title: Grammar in Numbers
subtitle: Arithmetic, Number Theory, and the Computational Grammar of Number
kicker: The second publication of a research program
author: Abed Kadaan
status: A research monograph. Not peer reviewed. Proofs marked “proved here” are self-checked and checked by computation on small cases; nearly all of the mathematics is classical, and it is labelled so. Machine claims name their toolchain and say whether they were measured, emulated or taken from a specification.
claims: This book does not claim new theorems of number theory, new algorithms, new complexity results or a replacement for any established theory. It claims a framework (arithmetic as computational grammars with four separable layers and converse admissibility), a vocabulary of failure (no solution versus non-unique), executable reference semantics with tests, and reproducible measurements of real machines. Every formal claim carries its evidence category and a ledger identifier.
description: An independent research monograph on numbers, numerals, arithmetic, number systems and number-theoretic algorithms as computational grammars: what an arithmetic expression asks for, when it is admissible, how it is represented, what machines actually do with it, and what it costs.

parts.title: What Is a Number?
parts.blurb: Number as object, value, symbol, numeral, count, position, state, address and machine representation — and what is assumed when we say that 1 + 1 = 2.

parts.title: Successor, Counting, and Numerical Transition
parts.blurb: 0 → 1 → 2 → 3 → 4: the smallest grammar, its converse, induction, recursion and the cost of counting.

parts.title: Digits, Numerals, and Positional Representation
parts.blurb: Numerals as programs: place value, canonical forms, zero's empty address, other digit grammars, and why 1 + 1 = 10₂ says nothing new about the value.

parts.title: Arithmetic as Formal Operations
parts.blurb: What an operation is: domains, closure, admissibility, operation contracts, and inverse operations as converse relations.

parts.title: Addition and Carry
parts.blurb: Addition from first principles; the carry automaton, its three-element monoid, and parallel prefix adders.

parts.title: Subtraction and Inverses
parts.blurb: Why 0 − 1 has no answer in ℕ and one in ℤ, and the other ways systems make subtraction total.

parts.title: Multiplication
parts.blurb: Multiplication as recursion, product and scaling; why ×0 gives 0; and the algorithms from shift-and-add to O(n log n).

parts.title: Division and the Boundary of Zero
parts.blurb: The central part: division as a converse, the image/kernel theorem, 1/0 versus 0/0, every way of giving 1/0 a value and what it costs, division with remainder, and the grammar of zero.

parts.title: Binary and Digital Arithmetic
parts.blurb: Bits are not numbers: words, masks, shifts, two's complement as truncated 2-adic integers, and arithmetic circuits.

parts.title: Machines That Compute Arithmetic
parts.blurb: An expression traced from characters to instructions, and what real compilers, languages, instruction sets and floating-point units do — measured, emulated, or specified.

parts.title: Number Systems as Computational Domains
parts.blurb: ℕ, ℤ, ℚ, ℝ, ℂ, ℤ/n, finite fields and p-adic integers: constructions, closure, inverses, order, representation and cost.

parts.title: Number Theory from First Principles
parts.blurb: Divisibility, primes and unique factorization; congruences, inverses and the Chinese remainder theorem; arithmetic functions and recurrences.

parts.title: Algorithms in Number Theory
parts.blurb: Euclid and its relatives, exponentiation by squaring, sieves, primality tests and factorization — each as a transition system with an invariant and a counted cost.

parts.title: The Complexity of Arithmetic
parts.blurb: Unit cost, word RAM and bit complexity kept apart; measured exponents; and what the shape of an evaluation does and does not change.

parts.title: Numerical Grammar and Computational Grammar Theory
parts.blurb: Exact correspondences, useful analogies and non-equivalences between this book and Computational Grammar Theory.

parts.title: Programming and AI Interfaces
parts.blurb: Operation contracts as an interface between a request and an execution system, measured against real toolchains; and the SDK.

parts.title: Findings, Limits, and Open Problems
parts.blurb: What has been proved, reproduced, implemented, observed, conjectured and left open.
